It can dif- ferentiate between simple cysts, solid nodules, or mixed cystic and solid nodules, although it cannot reliably distin- guish between benign and cancerous lesions. For the latter, fludeoxyglucose (18F) may be used to evaluate glucose metabolism by positron-emission tomography, although this method is not as economical as fine-needle aspiration biopsy. Radionuclide scanning with iodine isotopes may be used to identify whether a nodule is functioning (these are nearly always benign). Nodule size cannot be meas- ured accurately by radionuclide scanning. In established malignancy, surgery, followed by levothy- roxine replacement therapy, is the usual course (for further discussion of the treatment of thyroid cancer, see p.674). The treatment of non-toxic benign solitary nodules is a matter of dispute. Many prefer simply to monitor patients with benign solitary nodules. Alternatively suppressive therapy with doses of levothyroxine (or, less often, liothy- ronine) sufficient to suppress TSH production and reduce the size of the nodule has been widely practised, but results conflict as to whether such therapy is effective.3 A meta- analysis of 7 studies4 suggested that although levothyrox- ine treatment produced some benefit, the number of patients who responded was quite small. Another meta- analysis5 (which included 5 of the same studies and a later one) found an overall non-significant treatment response; the authors concluded that routine suppressive levothyrox- ine for single benign thyroid nodules could not be recom- mended, but that a subgroup of patients with small, solid nodules might benefit from therapy. US guidelines2 con- sider that it should generally be avoided, but may be con- sidered in patients from areas of iodine deficiency, young patients with small nodules, and in nodular goitres with no evidence of autonomous thyroid hormone production. There has been some concern about the possible risk of osteoporosis6 with levothyroxine (see Effects on the Bones, p.2171). An alternative to levothyroxine is treat- ment with potassium iodide, although it is somewhat less effective,7 and has adverse effects of its own.6 Sclerother- apy by alcohol injection can produce substantial reduc- tions,2,8,9 but is painful and requires considerable skill.1,2 Levothyroxine suppression therapy is effective in patients with diffuse non-toxic goitre, and may be of benefit in some patients with multinodular disease. However, many patients with large multinodular goitres have autonomous thyroid hormone production, and in such patients levothy- roxine is of no benefit and may cause overt hyperthy- roidism.
